newsitem.title: USA: China seen putting economy ahead of military might.
newsitem.headline: China seen putting economy ahead of military might.

text.p: China is expected to continue to emphasise economic growth and modernisation rather than military might as a foundation for national greatness, a U.S. Defence Department report said on Wednesday.
The report to Congress said China would probably build its military power at a measured pace, believing a more rapid or large-scale military buildup to be unnecessary.
It said China was developing and acquiring new fighter planes, sumbarines, improved naval air defences and short-range ballistic missiles.
Beijing's nuclear strategy probably would continue to emphasise development of nuclear retaliation ability to deter potential use of nuclear weapons by present nuclear states, the report said.
Releasing the report, Representative Floyd Spence, chairman of the House National Security Committee, said it showed the Chinese saw a need to create forces to offset U.S. military advantages.

"China has learned from the defeat of the Soviet Union in the Cold War that any challenge to America requires patience and strength over the long run," the South Carolina Republican said. "The strategic problems posed by an emerging and well-armed China may test us more than the Soviet Union ever did."
The Pentagon report said China's long-term goal was to become one of the world's great powers.
"Its leaders envision that, at some point during the first half of the 21st century, China will be securely established as the leading economic and political power in Asia," it said.

But it added: "Chinese statements and actions support the theory that China will continue to emphasise economic growth and economic modernisation rather than military might as a foundation for national greatness."

It said that as an emerging great power, China would probably build its military power to the point where it could engage and defeat any potential enemy within the region with its conventional forces, and deter any global strategic threat to China's national security.

"Evidence suggests, however, that China will develop her military strength at a measured pace," the report said. "A more rapid or large-scale military buildup is seen by Chinese leadership as unnecessary and detrimental to continued economic growth."
